hook: July 28, 2026: MCP's biggest revision ever — **the protocol went stateless**. Sessions, the handshake, and server-initiated callbacks are gone. Here's what changed and why it matters.

scenes.title: Date-stamped specs, negotiated per connection
scenes.sub: MCP versions itself like a standard, not like software
scenes.narration: MCP versions its specification by release date — 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25, then 2026-07-28 — and clients and servers NEGOTIATE which revision they speak during connection. Why dates and not semver: the protocol is a contract between independently shipped pieces — your server and someone else's host, built months apart — and the negotiation handshake exists precisely so a 2026 host can talk to a 2025 server while both stay honest about which rules apply. The 2026-07-28 revision — the fifth, published under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation — is the largest since authorization was added, and it's the one that changed the protocol's shape. Everything in this reel is about that revision.

items.s: Spec = living document · each revision names its rules explicitly
Client and server agree which revision to speak — mixed-era fleets interoperate deliberately
Fifth revision · maintainers called it a rebuild of the data-transfer mechanism

scenes.narration: The negotiation detail matters for migration planning: because revisions are negotiated, a fleet can migrate incrementally — new servers speak the new revision to new clients and the old one to old clients, with no big-bang cutover. That design choice is what makes the breaking changes in 2026-07-28 survivable. Also worth noting the governance shift: MCP now lives under the Agentic AI Foundation — a neutral home, multi-vendor governance — which is why the spec can make breaking moves like this at all: the process, not one vendor's roadmap, now defines the protocol's future. Keep the negotiation model in mind; it's the frame for everything that follows.

scenes.title: Sessions are gone. **Every request carries everything.**
scenes.sub: The headline change and the reason behind it
scenes.narration: Old MCP was stateful: an initialize handshake opened a session, the server issued a Mcp-Session-Id, and every subsequent request referenced that session — the server REMEMBERED negotiated state between calls. That broke at scale: load balancers needed sticky sessions or shared session stores — the most expensive part of running MCP servers at any real traffic. The 2026-07-28 core is stateless: the handshake and the session header are REMOVED outright, and every request is self-contained — it carries its own protocol version, client identity, and capability declarations in a metadata block. Any request can land on any server instance behind a plain round-robin load balancer. State didn't vanish; it moved from the transport into tool arguments, as explicit handles the model can see and manage.

cards.s: initialize handshake → session id → server remembers · sticky routing · shared session store
No handshake, no session header · request carries its own metadata · round-robin scales

scenes.narration: The architectural trade, stated fairly: the old model was friendlier to interactive servers — state persisted invisibly between calls, so an editor-automation server could hold selection and viewport context without burdening the model. The new model sacrifices that convenience for operability: stateless servers scale like normal REST services — no affinity, no shared store. And the 'explicit handles' pattern — state passed as ordinary tool arguments — has a hidden benefit the game-engine community noticed first: state becomes VISIBLE to the model, so the agent reasons about it instead of it hiding in a session the model can't see. Arguably better for agent cognition, definitely more migration work for stateful servers.

scenes.title: Server-initiated callbacks died — **MRTR is the replacement**
scenes.sub: The one pattern that replaced elicitation, sampling, and roots
scenes.narration: The old spec let servers initiate requests BACK to the client mid-conversation: elicitation — 'ask the user to confirm this destructive action'; sampling — 'have the model generate text for me'; roots — 'tell me which directories you expose'. All three required a held-open, bidirectional stream — impossible for a stateless server behind a load balancer. Enter Multi Round-Trip Requests — MRTR: the server returns an interim result marked input-required, carrying the questions it needs; the client gathers the answers — from the user, or by running a model completion — and RE-ISSUES the original request with the answers attached. A human approval step becomes a plain request-and-response pattern that survives load balancers and serverless runtimes. One round-trip pattern replaces three bespoke channels.

layers.s: User answers, or client runs a completion (the old 'sampling')
Same request re-issued with inputResponses attached (continuation state included)

scenes.narration: Walk the MRTR flow once and you'll never fear it again. Server: 'I need approval to delete record 42' — input-required, with the question structured. Client — the host — surfaces the question to the user, collects the answer, and re-sends the original tool call with the answer attached; servers that need to correlate the two attempts encode their own identifier in request state. Note how each old feature maps: elicitation becomes an input-required asking the user; sampling becomes an input-required asking for a model completion; roots become explicit arguments instead of a server query. And note the deprecation status precisely: roots, sampling, and logging are DEPRECATED with a twelve-month minimum runway — they still work, but new implementations must not adopt them. Sessions and the handshake, by contrast, were REMOVED — no grace period, because the old revisions still exist for old clients.

scenes.kicker: CHAPTER 4 · THE REST OF THE RELEASE
scenes.title: Extensions, hardened auth, and a formal lifecycle
scenes.narration: Beyond the stateless core, the revision shipped structure. Extensions framework: new capabilities now live as versioned extensions with reverse-DNS identifiers — Tasks — durable long-running work with poll-based result retrieval, contributed by AWS — and MCP Apps — servers shipping interactive, sandboxed UI alongside tool results. Both were officially folded in under this framework, keeping the core lean. Authorization hardened: OAuth aligned with real-world standards — RFC 9207 issuer validation, credentials bound to their issuer, and Dynamic Client Registration deprecated in favor of Client ID Metadata Documents. And a formal feature lifecycle: Active, Deprecated, Removed — with a minimum twelve-month window — plus cacheable capability catalogs with TTLs, modeled on HTTP caching. Tier 1 SDKs — TypeScript, Python, Go, C-sharp — shipped support at launch.

items.s: Reverse-DNS identifiers · independent versioning · Tasks (poll-based) + MCP Apps (sandboxed UI) graduated first
RFC 9207 issuer validation · Client ID Metadata Documents replace Dynamic Client Registration
Active → Deprecated (≥12 months) → Removed · cacheable catalogs with ttlMs

scenes.narration: The architect's takeaway list. Migration posture: if you run MCP servers, the stateless core plus MRTR is real work — the twelve-month deprecation window is for roots, sampling, and logging, but session reliance is a code change with no window, since old clients just negotiate old revisions. Check any server you depend on for migration activity — continued reliance on deprecated primitives after mid-2026 reads as a maintenance red flag. On extensions: the reverse-DNS, independently-versioned design means capabilities can evolve without bloating the core — watch Tasks for long-running agent work and MCP Apps for rich interactive results. And the catalog TTLs are a quiet cost win: clients cache capability lists instead of re-fetching per request. This is what a maturing protocol looks like: fewer features in the core, more discipline around them.

scenes.title: Spec understood. Let's USE the ecosystem instead of building it.
scenes.next: Reel 48 · Using Existing MCP Servers — reference servers, trust, gateways

recap: 2026-07-28: stateless core — handshake and sessions removed; every request self-contained with its own metadata; round-robin scaling
MRTR replaces all server-initiated callbacks: interim input_required result → client gathers answers → original call re-issued with responses
Roots, Sampling, Logging + HTTP+SSE deprecated (12-month floor); Tasks and MCP Apps graduated into a reverse-DNS extensions framework; OAuth hardened

quiz.q: Why did MCP remove protocol-level sessions?
opts: Sticky sessions and shared session stores were the most expensive part of operating MCP at scale — stateless requests scale behind plain load balancers
quiz.why: Operability drove the change: any request on any instance, no affinity, no shared store — MCP scales like a normal HTTP service.

quiz.q: How does MRTR replace sampling (server asks model to generate text)?
opts: The tool returns input_required; the client runs the model completion and re-issues the original call with the result attached
Servers now call the LLM directly
quiz.why: One round-trip pattern — pause, gather, retry — replaces every held-open bidirectional channel.

quiz.q: What's the difference between REMOVED and DEPRECATED in this revision?
opts: Sessions/handshake were removed outright (old revisions still serve old clients); Roots/Sampling/Logging were deprecated with a 12-month minimum window
quiz.why: Two different lifecycle outcomes in one release — and migration plans differ accordingly: session reliance has no grace period.

code.title: The migration checklist for a 2025-era server
code.body:
# From 2025-11-25 → 2026-07-28 — check your servers against this:

# REMOVED (no grace period):
#  □ Mcp-Session-Id header + any server-side session store
#  □ initialize/initialized handshake → send version/caps per-request in _meta
#  □ notifications/initialized, ping, logging/setLevel
#  □ HTTP GET endpoint + resources/subscribe → subscriptions/listen

# DEPRECATED (≥12 months, do NOT adopt in new code):
#  □ roots/list            → explicit path arguments
#  □ sampling/createMessage → MRTR input_required
#  □ elicitation           → MRTR input_required
#  □ logging               → server-side observability (AG-08)
#  □ HTTP+SSE transport    → Streamable HTTP
#  □ OAuth Dynamic Client Registration → Client ID Metadata Documents

# NEW (adopt):
#  □ Mcp-Method / Mcp-Name headers for gateway routing
#  □ ttlMs/cacheScope on capability catalogs
#  □ Long-running work → io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks (poll tasks/get)
#  □ Rich UI results → MCP Apps extension (sandboxed iframe)
annot: The checklist IS the reel: migration is mostly finding which of these your server touches
Tier 1 SDKs (TS/Python/Go/C#) support the new revision — often an SDK upgrade covers the mechanical parts
Stateful servers (editor automation, multi-call transactions) need the explicit-handle redesign — the real engineering

notes:
# MCP Spec Evolution

## Versioning
- Date-stamped revisions (2025-03-26 … 2025-11-25 → **2026-07-28**), negotiated per connection.
- Fifth revision; largest since auth; Linux Foundation (Agentic AI Foundation) governance.

## Stateless core
- REMOVED: sessions, `Mcp-Session-Id`, initialize/initialized handshake, ping, SSE resumability.
- Every request self-contained: version + identity + capabilities in `_meta`.
- Round-robin scaling; state → explicit handles in tool args (visible to the model).

## MRTR replaces server-initiated callbacks
- elicitation / sampling / roots → one pattern: `resultType: input_required` → client gathers → retry with `inputResponses`.

## Deprecated (12-month floor)
- Roots, Sampling, Logging, HTTP+SSE transport, OAuth DCR (→ Client ID Metadata Documents).

## New structure
- Extensions framework (reverse-DNS, versioned): Tasks (poll `tasks/get`), MCP Apps (sandboxed UI), Enterprise Managed Auth.
- Hardened OAuth (RFC 9207 issuer binding) · cacheable catalogs (ttlMs/cacheScope) · Mcp-Method/Name header routing.
- Tier 1 SDKs: TypeScript, Python, Go, C# (Rust beta).
